heading: Caching: Tac
summary: The same four annotations in the Tac service languages. CacheSettings is a modifier, so the service keeps its name, its client/services folder and its construction without arguments. The same annotations also work on the methods of an HTTPClient: the client class names its cache with CacheSettings, Cached keeps a read's answer, and ClearCache or UpdateCache on a write removes or replaces it (see the feature "Caching public reads").
body: CacheSettings selects configuration.caches.catalog from a configuration that the service creates itself. In JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart and Ruby, and in Go, Rust, C#, F#, Kotlin and Java services that run as WebAssembly, the Setup can leave caches out: Tachyon then keeps the cache in the browser Cache API. It loads the saved entries into memory before the services start, answers reads from memory and writes changes in the background. It enforces ttlMs, maxBytes (per value) and maxEntries (the least recently used entry goes first). Where the Cache API is missing, such as a plain-http address on a local network, the cache lives in memory only and the console says so once. In a Safari private window, and in any WebKit web view whose storage is not kept on disk, the browser drops the saved entries when the page reloads. The cache then starts empty and the next call runs the method again. Store rows stay. The Go and Java Setups leave caches out, because Go and Java run only as WebAssembly; their Cached reads come from the same memory copy through a synchronous storage host. Rust, C# and Kotlin keep an adapter in the example, because a native companion (Android Kotlin, or a native Swift, Rust or C# app) has no page storage. Its native build stops when a Cached, UpdateCache or ClearCache method uses a cache that no Setup in the service names, for example with "Android Kotlin services need a cache adapter in their Setup" (ADR 0059). The other Tac languages still name an adapter in their Setup, as shown. It adds no rule of its own about name endings or folders. Cached, UpdateCache and ClearCache behave exactly as they do in Yon. UpdateCache and ClearCache name find and map their arguments onto its key. JavaScript and TypeScript open the context in an async OnStart with the injected lifecycle signal. A native service owns its own BehaviorSignal. Its lifecycle hooks (such as OnStart) must be synchronous. So Swift, Kotlin, C#, Go and Java open the context in a synchronous OnStart. A Java Cached method returns Object, and the Behaviors.Context field stays inside the service. Rust builds it in new(), because a BehaviorContext field cannot be assigned through &self. The view reads the service's local state. Declaring a cache does not contact a server. The browser keeps only the values that Cached methods return, within the limits above. It runs only with public TAC_ configuration. Its bundle must never include the private credentials that a Yon cache adapter may hold. JS/TS bundle for every target, and Rust, Go, C#, Kotlin, Swift and Java reach the web, and every target that does not link them, as WebAssembly. A Swift Cached method is async and returns BehaviorJSON; on the web the page gets a promise, which settles at once when the method does not wait for the network. In a native app Tachyon runs the method to the end before the call returns. A Dart service owns its BehaviorSignal, as a native service does. It opens its context in a synchronous OnStart. The context is not a JSON value, so it stays inside Dart and the view never sees it. Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses Setup, CacheSettings and Cached in Lua Tac code with TY1308. Python has no tab either, because the build refuses CacheSettings and Cached in Python Tac code with TY1308. So Python Tac services cannot use caching yet. C++ has no tab here, because the build refuses Setup in C++ Tac code with TY1308. A synchronous C++ service method can still carry Cached, UpdateCache and ClearCache when its class has CacheSettings (ADR 0099).
